analysis.one_liner: Extends rare-disease drug monopolies by six months for applications filed during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in committee for the rest of the term.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drugs for rare diseases ('orphan drugs') get years of legal protection from competition after approval. This bill would add 180 days to those monopoly periods for any orphan drug whose application was filed during the COVID-19 emergency period, on the theory that the pandemic disrupted the drug development process. The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health subcommittee, where it stayed until the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers with orphan drug applications filed between December 2019 and the end of the COVID-19 emergency. Each qualifying drug would get an extra six months before cheaper generic or biosimilar versions could enter, across the full menu of exclusivity protections (12-year and 7-year orphan exclusivity, 5-year new-chemical-entity and 3-year clinical-data exclusivity, plus patent-related approval delays) [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds 180 days to the 12-year and 7-year orphan-drug exclusivity periods and the 5-year and 3-year new-drug exclusivity periods for qualifying rare-disease drugs, plus 180 days to related patent-delay periods [S3].

Applies to any orphan drug application submitted during the COVID-19 emergency period, defined as beginning December 1, 2019 and ending 120 days before the formal end of the public health emergency — a window of several years covering many applications [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients with rare diseases, who would pay the brand-name price for an extra six months before a cheaper generic or biosimilar could enter; insurers and public programs also absorb the higher costs.

drawbacks.text: Six more months without competition means rare-disease patients — many of whom already face very high drug prices — would wait longer for affordable versions of the same medicine [S3].
The extension is automatic for any application filed during the emergency window; the bill does not require a company to prove its own trial was actually delayed by the pandemic [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated rationale is real — COVID-19 genuinely slowed clinical trials and FDA review. But the remedy is a blanket six-month monopoly extension for every qualifying orphan drug, not a case-by-case adjustment, so the cost lands on patients regardless of how much any particular drug was disrupted. The gain flows to a small set of companies; the cost is spread across patients and payers for years of high prices.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which routed it to its Health subcommittee in April 2023, and it stayed there with no markup or vote until the term ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Gottheimer introduced the bill on March 27, 2023, joined by Rep. Don Bacon; it had one additional Democratic cosponsor, for a total of two [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on April 7, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Health — its last recorded action [S5].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never reached the House floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, patients and payers were spared six additional months of monopoly pricing on qualifying rare-disease drugs, and generic and biosimilar makers enter those markets on schedule. Brand-name orphan drug makers lose the extension they sought — modestly, since the bill was narrow.

for.name: Rep. Josh Gottheimer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on March 27, 2023

for.name: Rep. Don Bacon
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill's last action was its April 2023 referral to the Health subcommittee

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three supporters were two Democrats and one Republican, but it drew no floor action from either party.

industries.note: Qualifying orphan drugs would get 180 extra days of legal monopoly, during which patients pay the brand price with no generic or biosimilar alternative. The bill's gain to these companies is precisely the delay in cheaper competition.
Their entry into rare-disease drug markets would be pushed back six months; their interest in earlier entry runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.
